https://www.irishmirror.ie/lifestyle/tra.text: Throughout my years as a travel writer, I’ve not often felt more like I’m a time-travel writer - but in Gdansk the echoes of the past are hard to ignore. This beautiful city on Poland’s spectacular Baltic Coast stands proudly today as one of Central Europe’s must-visit destinations - but less than a century ago it all looked very different. Gdansk is the site where World War II broke out back on September 1, 1939 and later on in the conflict it suffered some catastrophic damage as the Soviet army laid waste to the region - destroying over 80% of the buildings in the historic Old Town and up to 95% of the central city as a whole. However, after the war the Polish authorities embarked on a meticulous campaign of reconstruction, with key landmarks lovingly restored to their former glory. And that spirit of resilience is still very much evident in the city today - an important message of hope in a world where devastating conflicts sadly continue to rage on. My history lesson took place on a three-day trip to the Gdansk region last month. And with Poland basking in record temperatures this summer - it averaged about 32C during my time there - it was certainly more pleasant than being in a stuffy classroom. If you are a WWII buff, then either the Museum of the Second World War or Westerplatte would be a perfect place to start. The former is just a short walk from the Old Town and is widely regarded as one of the foremost historical museum experiences in the world, with a huge range of immersive exhibits that trace the outline of the war, its toll on Poland and the human stories behind the conflict. I took a boat trip down the Motlawa river to the Westerplatte peninsula, which is where the first shots of WWII were fired, almost 87 years ago now. On that fateful day, a German battleship, the Schleswig-Holstein, opened fire on a military depot stationed there, marking Hitler’s intention to invade Poland. Despite Germany thinking that the battle to take Westerplatte would be over in hours, the brave Polish troops managed to hold out for seven days, repelling several assaults against far greater numbers and providing an inspiration to the public that still resonates to this day - commemorated forever in an imposing, 22m-high memorial called the Monument to the Defenders of the Coast. People in Poland didn’t exactly have it easy after the war either - they were put under communist rule and suffered decades of economic hardship and oppression. This sparked the Solidarity movement, which was founded in a Gdansk shipyard in 1980. Subsequent protests throughout the decade played a huge part in bringing about the eventual fall of communism in 1989, with the movement led by electrician Lech Walesa - who later became president, also lending his name to Gdansk’s airport. I paid a visit to the European Solidarity Centre in the city during my trip and it was a truly fascinating experience, with an abundance of exhibits detailing the movement’s leaders as they fought for freedom as well as the lives of ordinary people during such a tumultuous time. You also get a great sense of history just from walking around the cobbled streets of Gdansk’s Old Town - and indeed, the reconstruction of the city was so effective that it’s easy to forget most of the buildings around you had been reduced to rubble not so long ago. My very informative and knowledgeable guide Malgorzata (Margaret) was on hand to show me the many sights and we started on the Royal Way, so-called because in centuries past the king of Poland would take this route when visiting the city, entering through the imposing Highland Gate and making his way to the Green Gate by the river. Other landmarks on the street, called Dlugi Targ (Long Market), include the 17th-century Neptune’s Fountain, Artus Court, a former meeting place for merchants, and the stunning St Mary’s Church - one of the largest brick churches in the world. Also worth a look is the Main Town Hall, which offers the chance to head up to the top of its tower and enjoy panoramic views of the city. If climbing a few hundred steps is not quite your thing though, there is also plenty to see at the lower levels such as the spectacular Red Room, which boasts a Sistine Chapel-esque ceiling of frescoes in a Dutch Mannerist style. Continuing on down, we reached the Motlawa river and its incredibly picturesque waterfront promenade, which was one of the highlights of my visit with its unforgettable backdrop of colourful townhouses and ornate buildings on either side of the river along with bustling cafes and restaurants. Here, you will also found the Gdansk Crane, one of the city’s most iconic landmarks. It dates from the 15th century and was the largest medieval port crane in Europe. These days it houses an exhibition showcasing Gdansk’s history as a shipping and maritime trade hub. Two or three days in the Old Town would be time very well spent indeed, but there is also plenty more to see beyond Gdansk’s historic centre. We took a short train ride out to the leafy suburb of Oliwa, which acts as a relaxing, more nature-filled counterpoint to the crowds of tourists in the city (which are in turn far more manageable than in the usual overcrowded European hotspots). The sprawling Oliwa Park made for an extremely pleasant stroll, with plenty of shade from the sun being an added bonus. We stopped at a local market where I had my first taste of pierogi - the famous Polish dumplings which come with a variety of fillings. I tried a vegetarian one and one with duck and only for the fact that lunch was booked nearby stopped me from going back and filling up my plate with more because they were simply delicious. The park dates back to the 12th and 13th centuries when a Cistercian monastery was founded in the area and a couple of striking remnants from that era remain - the Abbot’s Palace and Oliwa Cathedral, the latter holding the honour of being the longest Cistercian church in the world as well as housing a humongous organ with thousands of pipes. Also noticeable was a very Irish-looking name on the church walls - Edward O’Rourke, who was a Belarus-born priest with ancestral links to the Flight of the Wild Geese, the departure of Irish Jacobite families in the 17th century after the end of the Williamite War in Ireland. Gdansk is also part of what is known as the Tricity area along with the nearby cities of Gdynia and Sopot, and both of these are also easily accessible by train. In fact, Gdynia is celebrating its centenary this year so there is no better time to visit - not that you really needed an excuse, as in those 100 years it has transformed itself from a tiny fishing village to one of the Baltic Coast’s most popular and distinctive seaside destinations. Part of Gdynia’s distinctiveness is its modernist city centre. Just last week it was inscribed on the World Heritage List, recognising its unique whitewashed facades, curved balconies and streamlined, ocean-liner-inspired buildings - so all the more reason to celebrate. Down at the marina, you will find ships of every shape and size, with many converted to museums such as the ORP Błyskawica, the world’s oldest preserved destroyer, and the sailing ship Dar Pomorza. The Naval Museum is also well worth popping into, with exhibits on Gdynia’s seafaring history plus an open-air display including a tour of a retired submarine. Meanwhile, fans here of EPIC, the Irish Emigration Museum, will definitely want to give the Gdynian counterpart a visit, with its engaging approach to telling the story of Polish emigration through the years. And if you’re in the mood to just chill out on the beach, Gdynia boasts some golden sand that is equal to anything you’d get in Spain or Portugal - with a fraction of the crowds too. The same is true on the beaches in Sopot, which is known as the ‘Polish Riviera’, and although you might find more people here there is still lots of space. Sopot’s other claim to fame is the longest wooden pier in Europe, which stretches over 500m into the Baltic Sea, with opportunities to take speedboat trips, cruises and much more. There’s also Monte Cassino, a vibrant pedestrian street packed with boutiques and cafes, plus the iconic Crooked House landmark. I also want to highlight that the food I had throughout my Polish sojourn was uniformly excellent. Apart from the aforementioned pierogi, I indulged in a variety of fantastic seafood dishes at various restaurants, and it would be pretty impossible to choose a favourite between the rainbow trout, sea bream, mussels in pomodoro sauce, Kashubian cod and pan-seared zander. My mouth is watering again just writing this... A final word goes to amber - the fossilised tree resin is everywhere in Gdansk, and has been harvested and traded in the region for thousands of years, leading to the city being known as the ‘World Amber Capital’. There is a Museum of Amber as well as stalls across the city selling amber jewellery products. And in a way it is rather fitting - because Gdansk itself is a real gem, and should be at the top of your list if you’re looking for the next city break to discover. GETTING THERE: Ryanair offer direct flights from Dublin to Gdansk. WHERE TO STAY: The Hampton by Hilton is a modern and very comfortable hotel located in the Old Town, just a short walk away from the major attractions. WHERE TO EAT: Recommended restaurants include Rekawiczka, Gdanski Bowke, Canis and Chleb i Wino (all Gdansk) plus Viceversa (Gdynia) and Tu Mozna Marzyc (Oliwa). DATE Wednesday, July 29, 2026 at 2:00 p.m. ET CALL PARTICIPANTS President and Chief Executive Officer - Aaron Berg Executive VP, President of Research & Development and Chief Scientific Officer - Steven Ketchum Chief Financial Officer - Pete Fishman Investor Relations - Devin Sullivan TAKEAWAYS Total Net Revenue -- $42.2 million, decreasing 42% from the prior year period primarily due to the inclusion of a $25 million upfront licensing payment in 2025. U.S. Product Revenue -- $32.2 million, representing a 12% decline reflecting ongoing pricing pressure from generic competitors despite higher product volumes. Europe Product Revenue -- $5.4 million, consisting entirely of supply shipments to Recordati and increasing 11% from the first quarter of 2026. Rest-of-World Revenue -- $1.4 million, declining from $3.5 million due to normal variability in partner purchasing patterns and shipment timing. Licensing and Royalty Revenue -- $3.1 million, reflecting royalties from the Recordati agreement and partially offsetting the absence of the prior year's upfront payment. Operating Loss -- $12.0 million, narrowing by 25% from $16.0 million as lower operating expenses offset increased cost of goods sold. Net Loss -- $7.7 million, improving from a net loss of $14.1 million in the second quarter of 2025. Cash and Investments -- $314.6 million, increasing from $303 million at year-end 2025 with the company remaining debt free. Operating Expenses -- $27.0 million, a 59% reduction reflecting the completion of the global restructuring plan and a $70 million annual cost savings initiative. Selling, General and Administrative Expense -- $22.2 million, declining 43% year over year following organizational resizing. Research and Development Expense -- $4.8 million, remaining consistent with ongoing global regulatory support and scientific commitments. Inventory -- $164.1 million, declining by $31.8 million from December 31, 2025, through disciplined purchasing and inventory management. Working Capital -- $439 million, supporting the company's leaner cost structure and financial flexibility. U.S. Market Share -- 48%, increasing from 43% as of June 30, 2025, despite multi-source generic competition in the icosapent ethyl market. U.S. Branded Prescriptions -- 14% increase year over year, demonstrating continued commercial execution in the domestic market. Europe In-Market Demand -- 69% increase year over year, supported by commercial launches in 11 European countries including a recent launch in Romania. Global Partner In-Market Demand -- 59% increase year over year, driven by the combined efforts of Recordati and six other commercial partnerships. China In-Market Volume -- 90% year-to-date growth, reflecting significant demand in the Asian territory. Full-Year 2026 Cash Outlook -- 10% expected growth, compared to the cash balance as of December 31, 2025. Annual Cost Savings -- $70 million, with the company confirming the full achievement of its previously announced target. Global Commercial Footprint -- 22 countries, representing the current reach of VASCEPA and VAZKEPA through partnered and company-managed channels. U.S. IPE Market Growth -- 3%, reflecting the expansion of the overall icosapent ethyl market during the second quarter. Cost of Goods Sold -- $27.2 million, rising 22% due to higher product volumes and the impact of regaining an exclusive PBM relationship in late 2025. Positive Cash Flow -- $7 million, representing the third consecutive quarter of positive cash flow from operations. Non-GAAP Net Income -- $790,000, adjusting for stock-based compensation, restructuring charges, and litigation-related expenses. Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected] RISKS Fishman stated, "U.S. product revenue declined to $32.2 million from $36.5 million in Q2 2025, driven by ongoing pricing pressure in the competitive generic market," noting that while volumes increased, net pricing remains under significant pressure. SUMMARY Management reported a shift toward a scalable business model following the completion of restructuring activities and the one-year anniversary of its international partnership strategy. Amarin Corporation plc ( AMRN +0.21% ) is maintaining its lead in the U.S. icosapent ethyl market while transitioning to a royalty and supply-based revenue stream in Europe through its partner Recordati. Financial results reflected narrowed operating losses and three consecutive quarters of positive operating cash flow. Management stated that the organizational focus has shifted to supporting global commercial partners through regulatory, scientific, and medical expertise. CEO Berg stated, "we continue to work closely with our exclusive financial adviser, Barclays, as we actively evaluate additional potential opportunities to enhance shareholder value." Recordati has positioned VAZKEPA as a priority brand in its European cardiovascular portfolio, leveraging established infrastructure in Italy and Spain to drive early uptake. The 2026 ACCAHA multi-society dyslipidemia guideline and the cardiovascular kidney metabolic syndrome guideline both formally recommend high-dose icosapent ethyl for high-risk patients. Amarin will support its Australian partner, CSL Seqirus, at the Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand Annual Scientific Meeting to present data on secondary prevention after myocardial infarction. CFO Fishman indicated that while the company holds authorization for share repurchases through the second quarter of 2029, capital deployment is being evaluated across multiple forms. Management confirmed that U.S. exclusivity with key payers is expected to remain in place through the end of 2026, helping stabilize domestic volumes. The company plans to participate in the European Society of Cardiology Congress in Munich, where it will present five scientific abstracts including new REDUCE-IT analyses. INDUSTRY GLOSSARY VASCEPA / VAZKEPA : A prescription medication containing icosapent ethyl used to reduce cardiovascular risk and treat severe hypertriglyceridemia. IPE : Icosapent ethyl, the active ingredient in VASCEPA, which is a highly purified form of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA). REDUCE-IT : A landmark cardiovascular outcomes trial that demonstrated significant risk reduction with high-dose icosapent ethyl. PBM : Pharmacy Benefit Manager, a third-party administrator of prescription drug programs that negotiates with pharmaceutical manufacturers. Apo B : Apolipoprotein B, a protein that is a primary component of many lipoproteins and serves as a biomarker for cardiovascular risk. Residual Cardiovascular Risk : The risk of cardiovascular events that remains despite achieving target levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol with statin therapy. Full Conference Call Transcript Operator: Good morning, and welcome to Amarin Corporation's conference call to discuss its Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results. Please note that this conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Devin Sullivan, Investor Relations for Amarin. Devin Sullivan Thank you for your time and attention this morning as we discuss Amarin's 2026 second quarter financial results. On today's call are Aaron Berg, President and Chief Executive Officer; Steve Ketchum, President, Research & Development and Chief Scientific Officer; and Pete Fishman, Chief Financial Officer Other members of the senior management team will be available as needed during the Q&A session following the prepared remarks. Aaron will provide a state-of-the-company update. Steve will review recent medical and regulatory activities, and Pete will discuss the numbers. Before we begin, I'd like to remind everyone that today's press release and related Quarterly Report on Form 10-Q will be available on the Investor Relations section of the company's website, www.amarincorp.com, as well as a replay of this call shortly after its completion. Please be aware that during this call, we may make certain statements related to our business that are deemed forward-looking statements under federal securities laws. These statements are not guarantees of future performance, but rather are subject to a variety of risks and uncertainties. Our actual results could differ materially from expectations reflected in any forward-looking statements. Additionally, we assume no obligation to update these statements as circumstances change. For a discussion of the material risks and important factors that could affect our actual results, please refer to our SEC filings, which are available either on our company website or the Securities and Exchange Commission's EDGAR system. With that said, I'd now like to turn the call over to Amarin's President and CEO, Aaron Berg. Aaron, please go ahead. Aaron Berg: Thanks, Devin, and thank you all for joining us today. Q2 2026 marked an inflection point for Amarin, highlighting the 1-year anniversary of our dual commercial strategy that combines continued execution of our U.S. business with a fully partnered international commercial platform. The successful implementation of these actions has resulted in a scalable business model while defining a clear path towards sustainable growth and profitability. We're seeing a promising early-stage international sales trajectory in a number of markets where there remains significant unmet need and long-term potential for VAZKEPA while preserving a leading U.S. presence for VASCEPA, supported by a financial foundation that includes a growing cash position and no debt. Our restructuring activities are now complete, resulting in a significantly lower cost base. This refined organizational structure and expense framework will enhance our ability to efficiently execute our long-term growth strategy. As you may have noticed in our press release, we're now able to provide an outlook for certain key metrics for full-year 2026, reflecting the clarity afforded by our new operating model and the strong partnerships that make up its foundation. This underscores how far the business has progressed in the past year while validating our global go-to-market initiatives and reinforcing the continued outstanding execution of our talented, committed team. As of June 30, 2026, VASCEPA was commercially available in 22 countries via both our fully partnered international commercial strategy and company-managed U.S. presence. Our accelerating international growth is being driven primarily by our exclusive license and supply agreement with Recordati, which covers 59 countries across Europe, as well as our 6 other commercial partnerships in the rest of the world that cover regions, including Canada, China, Israel, the Middle East, Asia, Australia and New Zealand. Across this combined global partner network, in-market demand for VASCEPA rose by 59% in cumulative year-over-year volume as of June 30 compared to the same period last year. As of the end of Q2, VAZKEPA is commercialized in 11 countries in Europe, including a recent launch in Romania, and Recordati continues to invest meaningfully with pricing, reimbursement, market access and adoption advancing in numerous additional countries across the licensed territory. Under Recordati's leadership, VAZKEPA is in an early but promising stage of commercialization in Europe's large cardiovascular market, where the disease affects an estimated 62 million people and carries an annual economic burden of approximately EUR 282 billion across the European Union. In-market demand in Europe for VAZKEPA under the Recordati partnership rose by 69% in Q2 2026 from Q2 2025. Spain and the U.K., though early, are leading commercial adoption, providing a strong foundation for future growth as pricing, reimbursement, and commercialization efforts continue across the broader territory. In Italy, where Recordati has one of the country's most established pharmaceutical commercial organizations, VAZKEPA launched with significant commercial support and has demonstrated strong early uptake. VAZKEPA is positioned by Recordati as a priority brand in its cardiovascular portfolio, backed by an expanded cardiovascular commercial infrastructure across Europe, including dedicated field representatives, medical science liaisons and marketing investment. In its 2025 annual report, Recordati referred to VAZKEPA as a best-in-class treatment option that complements its existing cardiovascular portfolio, is supported by a robust clinical data package and makes a meaningful impact for cardiovascular patients with residual cardiovascular risk. While driving utilization in launch markets, Recordati is actively progressing pricing, reimbursement, and market access across additional territories, building a meaningful base for long-term royalty and milestone growth as additional countries come online. While very early, the commercial performance since the June 2025 licensing transaction is encouraging in that Recordati's established cardiovascular infrastructure, broader geographic footprint, and tremendous execution have unlocked substantially greater value from VAZKEPA than would have otherwise been possible had Amarin continued VAZKEPA commercialization throughout Europe alone. The commercial momentum generated by Recordati thus far materially exceeds historical European growth rates achieved by Amarin prior to the licensing transaction. As a reminder, European markets each follow their own regulatory process for pricing, reimbursement and market access, so commercial launches can progress at different speeds and under varying requirements across countries despite an overarching EU framework. In the U.S., our core business continues to serve as a highly efficient tax-generating base with VASCEPA retaining a leading position in the icosapent ethyl market despite ongoing generic pressure. We continue to expect to maintain our exclusivity with key payers through the end of 2026. The overall U.S. IPE market, based on third-party data, rose by 3% in Q2 2026 compared to Q2 2025. VASCEPA's share of the market rose to 48% as of June 30, 2026, up from 43% in the same period last year. Despite continued pricing pressure, VASCEPA branded prescriptions increased 14% year-over-year in the second quarter of 2026, reflecting continued commercial execution in a competitive market. We expect U.S. volumes to remain stable through the end of 2026. Outside of Europe and the U.S., we continue to support our partners in advancing regulatory submissions in various other countries across Asia. We recently received approvals in Singapore and South Korea and look forward to the launches in these territories in 2027. As our international footprint continues to expand, the work of our medical affairs, regulatory, and R&D teams becomes increasingly important. Beyond supporting Amarin's own scientific objectives, these teams provide critical expertise to our commercialization partners around the world to contribute to our joint success, helping them navigate local regulatory requirements, continuing to contribute to an already robust library of scientific evidence supporting the benefits and unique attributes of icosapentethyl, engaging with key scientific leaders, supporting reimbursement discussions, and preparing for successful product launches. Through scientific exchange, congress participation, publication support, medical education initiatives and ongoing regulatory collaboration, these teams help ensure that our partners have access to the latest data and insights supporting VASCEPA as they work to improve access for patients in their respective markets. Police were called to the Brinell School in Fagersta shortly after 14:00 local time (13:00 BST) on Friday, where officers arrested an 18-year-old man. In an update on Friday, police said officers fired at the suspect before arresting and detaining him. He has not been named. Two teenage boys were seriously injured in the attack. Another person had minor injuries. Eight other schools in the area were placed under lockdown measures - which have now been lifted - while a state of high alert was declared in the VÃ¤stmanland region following the attack. Sweden's public broadcaster reported that the suspect was wearing a helmet. Local media also said he was a former student. Police said officers were now working to establish possible motives, adding that there was currently no danger to the public. In a post on X, Sweden's Prime Minsiter Ulf Kristersson described the attack as a "serious incident," and said "we do not know what lies behind the act, but we know that police are working very intensively". Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf said he received the news "with dismay and sadness". In a statement, he said: "My thoughts are with those directly affected, as well as their families and loved ones." Students at Brinell School had only just returned to the classroom following the summer break, with the new term beginning either on Monday or Wednesday this week, depending on the academic year. The school has just under 500 students on its roster, according to SVT, and is located 170km (105 miles) north-west of the capital, Stockholm. Sweden has experienced a number of attacks on educational institutions in recent years. The country experienced its worst-ever mass shooting in 2025 , where 11 people, including the gunman, died at an adult education centre in Ãrebro. This led to the government tightening the country's gun laws after it was found that the suspect legally owned four rifles, three of which were found in the school where attack took place. Two teachers were killed in a violent attack on a secondary school in Malmo in 2022 - an 18-year-old student later confessed to the attack. By Shweta Ghadashi August 28, 2026 Fjord Trailer_pic courtesy Youtube Neon has released the first official trailer for Fjord , the upcoming drama from Romanian filmmaker Cristian Mungiu. Starring Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve, the film explores family, religion, suspicion and the difficult line between genuine concern and prejudice. Fjord is scheduled to arrive in cinemas on October 9, 2026. The story follows the Gheorghiu family, led by Mihai, a religious Romanian father played by Sebastian Stan, and Lisbet, his Norwegian wife played by Renate Reinsve. The couple moves with their five children to Lisbet’s hometown in Norway and settles in a small coastal village surrounded by mountains and fjords. The family initially sees the move as a chance to begin a new life. Their children soon become friends with children from the neighbouring Halberg family, helping the Gheorghius become part of the local community. However, their peaceful start does not last long. The family’s strict beliefs and behaviour begin to attract attention in the village. The situation becomes much more serious when allegations of abuse involving the children are raised. The Gheorghius suddenly find themselves under close examination from neighbours and authorities. The trailer does not appear to give viewers a simple answer about what really happened. Instead, the film seems to focus on how quickly people can form opinions when they do not understand another family’s culture, beliefs or way of life. It also raises the question of whether the community is genuinely trying to protect children or allowing suspicion and prejudice to influence its actions. Sebastian Stan plays Mihai, whose strong religious beliefs become an important part of the conflict. Renate Reinsve’s Lisbet has a different connection to the village because she grew up there. Her position becomes increasingly complicated as her family faces growing pressure from the community. The cast also includes Lisa Carlehed, Henrikke Lund Olsen, Vanessa Ceban, Jonathan Ciprian Breazu, Ellen Dorrit Petersen, Lisa Loven Kongsli and Markus Tønseth. Fjord is written and directed by Cristian Mungiu, a two time Cannes Film Festival Palme d’Or winner. The film was shot entirely in Norway, using its fjords, mountains and remote coastal locations to create an increasingly tense atmosphere. The beautiful surroundings contrast with the growing conflict faced by the family. As suspicion spreads, the close community begins to feel less welcoming and more isolating. Fjord explores questions about parenting, religion, cultural differences and protecting children, while also examining how genuine concern can sometimes turn into unfair judgment. The film arrives in cinemas on October 9, 2026. Home Paid news feed Foto Agerpres Press Monitoring Bucharest Phone: +4 021.2076.110 CultMin Demeter on Romania attending Frankfurt Book Fair 2028: I am waiting for a Publishers' Association proposal Category: English Date: 2026-10-12 20:08:33 Foto: Silviu MATEI / AGERPRES Photo The interim Minister of Culture, Andras Istvan Demeter, on Monday said that he is waiting for a proposal from the Romanian Publishers' Association (AER) to deal with Romania's participation in the International Book Fair in Frankfurt 2028, as guest of honour, otherwise this responsibility will be entrusted to the Office of Film and Cultural Investments (OFIC). Demeter participated in a news conference dedicated to preparing Romania's participation, as guest of honour, in the International Book Fair in Frankfurt 2028, a conference in which he presented the framework for organising the schedule, the role of the organisations involved and voiced support for the proposal for OFIC to manage the schedule. Demeter's proposal was met by the refusal of AER, with the vice-president of the publishers' guild, Lidia Bodea, reproaching the Ministry of Culture for not inviting the association to the discussions on Romania's participation in the 80th edition of the Frankfurt Fair. 'I am waiting for only one thing: AER - which theoretically meets the legal conditions and requirements - either makes me a proposal to be the first violin, the second violin and which it wants and can assume, so that it can be integrated. In the absence of such proposal, I see no other solution than to go with the only institutional approach I was trying to talk about, namely to designate the only entity that could manage this problem, and then it will carry out the project from one end to the other with the involvement of guilds, associative organisations, creative unions, including the Writers' Union, with all its subsidiaries, and to bring together all these ideas - which for the time being are rather sporadic - and interests. Here we are talking about industries. Even the Frankfurt Book Fair is an industry. They are interested in organising an event, in renting the stand, in collecting the money and all finishing a success story. It's about industries,' Demeter told AGERPRES. The minister added that he invited the Romanian Publishers' Association to discussions. 'I have invited them. I participated in the discussions. I waited. They said they waited too. Well, today we broke the ice, so that everyone knows that the other is waiting. But the law is the same since 2003. We should know it just as well. The ministry organises, with consultation, or it can entrust them with organising themselves with the support of the ministry. We know these things. We hide behind our fingers when we say 'I waited for you to invite me'. As long as I, personally, believe that I am the only minister who participated in Bucharest, in Sfantul Gheorghe, in Cluj, in Mures, in I don't know how many fairs in which I had meetings with the organisers of the fairs, with the participating publishers, to discuss Frankfurt. Starting with Bookfest. All these things could or should have been known. Well, no problem. What has happened has passed, from this moment we can at least take note of each other and, by elimination, there is only AER, from the point of view of the (book) industry, if it has the capacity to manage the entire project,' Demeter said. He added that the budget of the project will be provided by the government, but there will also have to be 'an attracted party, because the government does not provide the entire amount.' Demeter, however, expressed his distrust of AER's taking up the management of the schedule. 'AER will tell me what ARTEXIM or the National Library will have said: 'we are only good at books, we are not interested in the rest'. Good. And then I ask you: but what about the rest? Who does the rest? OFIC is a kind of institutional project manager. It could have been anyone else. It wasn't meant to be. I repeat, if AER comes with this proposal to manage the whole, I have no problem with OFIC returning to its priorities. And then we will make a government decision by which we entrust AER with this responsibility,' the culture minister also said. In his turn, the manager of OFIC, Valentin Savu, told AGERPRES that the appointment of the Film and Cultural Investments Office as manager of Romania's participation in the International Book Fair in Frankfurt 2028 was only a proposal of the Ministry of Culture. Savu went on to say that OFIC was appointed a week ago and 'thrown, unfortunately, into a war of intentions' to which it tries not to respond. 'Last week, the culture minister made a proposal to OFIC. That should be discussed from the perspective of OFIC, as we have done with the Alliance of Romanian Film Producers, with the professional associations. There can be no such designation outside of a dialogue. The Ministry of Culture will have to coordinate this dialogue, in its capacity as the supervisory authority. From my perspective, that of the OFIC manager, such a proposal - unlike my colleagues who refused such a proposal - cannot be refused,' Savu said. He added that the Frankfurt 2028 project is one 'of overwhelming importance, especially to the book market, and also to the entire Romanian culture.' 'And we have to look at what has happened in the last five years, past the COVID pandemic, at the format of the Frankfurt Book Fair. It has changed, we are no longer talking about a book fair in the sense of the seven, five days of a book fair, but we are talking about a real 'cultural capital' in another country. For such a programme of national interest, a government decision is needed (...) everyone needs to contribute to this programme. The government decision cannot be drawn up, issued if we do not have a programme, which should be made by the Ministry of Culture, together with the one who will be designated to coordinate, together with all the associative organisations, from publishing houses, to translators, booksellers, writers, authors,' Savu said. During the meeting, representatives of the National Library of Romania, the Romanian Cultural Institute (ICR), ARTEXIM, the National Centre of Filmmaking (CNC) and the Administration of the National Cultural Fund (AFCN) presented how the institutions they represent can contribute to the development of the Frankfurt 2028 programme, without taking up the responsibility of managing the programme. Under the scheme, Nvidia chips made in Taiwan could be sold to Chinese companies if they were imported to the US first for a security review. This also made them subject to a 25% tariff under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, which was aimed at dealing with imports that threaten national security. The commerce secretary could then grant an export licence to sell the chips to China. Two Democratic senators are now demanding Trump officials retain all records relating to the scheme as the fallout from now former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy continues to grow.
